title: Shannon Entropy: Measuring Uncertainty
hook: Entropy quantifies the average surprise or uncertainty in a random variable. It tells us how many bits are needed on average to encode outcomes. Understanding entropy is key to data compression and communication limits.

steps.explain: Entropy is the negative sum of each probability times its base-2 logarithm.
By convention, zero probability contributes nothing to entropy.
If an outcome is certain, there is no uncertainty, so entropy is zero.
For equally likely outcomes, entropy is maximized and equals log2(n).

explorations.title: Certainty gives zero entropy
explorations.predict: Set n=2, p₁=1, p₂=0. What is the entropy?
explorations.why: When one outcome is certain, there is no uncertainty, so entropy is zero.

explorations.title: Four equally likely outcomes give two bits
explorations.predict: Set n=4, all probabilities equal to 0.25. What is the entropy?
explorations.why: For four equally likely outcomes, entropy is log2(4) = 2 bits.

limitation: This demonstration assumes independent outcomes and uses a small number of outcomes. Real-world distributions may have many outcomes and dependencies.
misconception: Entropy is not the same as the number of outcomes; it depends on their probabilities. A distribution with many outcomes but one very likely outcome can have low entropy.

claims.text: Entropy is defined as H = -∑ p_i log2 p_i.
Entropy is zero when one outcome has probability 1.
Entropy is maximized when all outcomes are equally likely.

selftests.why: Two equally likely outcomes give 1 bit of entropy.
Certainty (one outcome with probability 1) gives zero entropy.
Zero probabilities do not affect entropy; this is equivalent to two equally likely outcomes.
